# Shivam Thakur — Full Stack Developer

> applications end to end with React, Next.js and Node.js. This site is his portfolio:
> case studies of shipped products, the services he offers, and practical articles on
> modern web development. The whole site is static HTML with clean, extensionless URLs.

## Learn

- [Learn](https://shivamthakur.me/learn): free learning hub.
- [DSA Master: Data Structures & Algorithms in JavaScript](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master): DSA Master is a free, 28-chapter course that teaches data structures and algorithms in JavaScript from first principles. Each chapter explains one topic with real-life analogies, dry runs and runnable code, then ends with revision notes, a cheat sheet, 20 MCQs, 20 coding problems, interview questions and project ideas.
- [Chapter 1: Big-O Notation and Time Complexity in JavaScript](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/big-o-notation-time-complexity): Big-O notation describes how an algorithm's running time or memory grows as the input grows, ignoring constants and machine speed. This chapter explains what data structures and algorithms are, why we measure growth instead of timing code, every common complexity class from O(1) to O(n!), and the real cost of JavaScript's built-in methods.
- [Chapter 2: Recursion in JavaScript: Call Stack, Base Cases and Memoization](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/recursion-in-javascript): Recursion is a technique where a function solves a problem by calling itself on a smaller version of the same problem until it reaches a base case. This chapter covers the anatomy of a recursive function, what happens on the call stack, why naive Fibonacci is exponential, how memoization fixes it, and when iteration is the better choice.
- [Chapter 3: Arrays and Strings in JavaScript: Two Pointers, Sliding Window and Prefix Sums](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/arrays-and-strings-javascript): Arrays store elements in contiguous memory, which gives O(1) access by index, while JavaScript strings are immutable sequences of characters. This chapter explains how dynamic arrays grow, the true cost of every array operation, and the four patterns that solve most array and string problems: two pointers, sliding window, prefix sums and difference arrays.
- [Chapter 4: Hashing in JavaScript: Hash Tables, Map, Set and Collisions](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/hashing-hash-table-javascript): A hash table stores key-value pairs by running each key through a hash function that computes where it belongs, which gives O(1) average lookup, insertion and deletion. This chapter builds a hash table from scratch, explains collisions, chaining, open addressing and resizing, compares Object, Map, Set and WeakMap, and teaches the five hashing patterns used in interviews.
- [Chapter 5: Linked Lists in JavaScript: Singly, Doubly and Circular](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/linked-list-javascript): A linked list is a sequence of nodes where each node stores a value and a pointer to the next node, so elements do not need to sit next to each other in memory. This chapter builds singly and doubly linked lists in JavaScript, compares them with arrays, and works through the classic problems: reversal, merging, middle node, cycle detection and removal.
- [Chapter 6: Stacks and Queues in JavaScript: LIFO, FIFO and Deques](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/stack-and-queue-javascript): A stack is a last-in-first-out (LIFO) collection where you add and remove from the same end; a queue is first-in-first-out (FIFO), adding at the back and removing from the front. This chapter implements both in JavaScript, introduces the deque, explains why Array.shift makes a slow queue, and shows where these structures power real software.
- [Chapter 7: Fast and Slow Pointers: Floyd's Cycle Detection Explained](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/fast-and-slow-pointers): The fast and slow pointer technique moves two pointers through a sequence at different speeds, usually one step and two steps at a time. If there is a cycle the fast pointer eventually meets the slow one. This chapter proves why Floyd's algorithm works, finds the cycle's start and length, and applies the pattern to arrays, numbers and palindrome lists.
- [Chapter 8: Trees in JavaScript: Binary Trees, Traversals and Binary Search Trees](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/binary-tree-and-bst-javascript): A tree is a hierarchical structure of nodes where each node has children and exactly one parent, except the root. A binary search tree keeps smaller values on the left and larger values on the right, which allows O(log n) search when it is balanced. This chapter covers tree vocabulary, the four traversal orders, recursive tree metrics, BST operations and self-balancing trees.
- [Chapter 9: Heaps and Priority Queues in JavaScript: Min-Heap, Max-Heap and Top-K](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/heap-priority-queue-javascript): A heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array where every parent is smaller (min-heap) or larger (max-heap) than its children, so the minimum or maximum is always at the top. This chapter builds a generic heap in JavaScript, explains sift-up, sift-down and O(n) heapify, and covers the Top-K and two-heap median patterns.
- [Chapter 10: Trie Data Structure in JavaScript: Prefix Trees and Autocomplete](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/trie-data-structure): A trie, or prefix tree, stores strings character by character so that words with the same prefix share the same path from the root. It answers prefix questions, such as which words start with a given prefix, in time proportional to the prefix length. This chapter builds a trie in JavaScript and applies it to autocomplete, word break and grid word search.
- [Chapter 11: Graphs in JavaScript: Adjacency Lists, BFS and DFS](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/graph-bfs-dfs-javascript): A graph is a set of vertices connected by edges, and it can model networks, maps, dependencies and social connections. This chapter covers graph vocabulary and types, how to represent a graph with an adjacency list or matrix, depth-first and breadth-first search with visited tracking, connected components, grid problems and cycle detection in directed and undirected graphs.
- [Chapter 12: Shortest Path Algorithms: Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford and Floyd-Warshall](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/shortest-path-dijkstra-bellman-ford): Shortest path algorithms find the cheapest route between vertices in a weighted graph. Dijkstra's algorithm is fastest for non-negative weights, Bellman-Ford handles negative weights and detects negative cycles, and Floyd-Warshall computes the distance between every pair of vertices. This chapter implements all three in JavaScript and gives a decision framework for choosing between them.
- [Chapter 13: Topological Sort and Minimum Spanning Trees: Kahn's, Kruskal's and Prim's](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/topological-sort-minimum-spanning-tree): Topological sort orders the vertices of a directed acyclic graph so that every dependency comes before what depends on it, as in build systems and course schedules. A minimum spanning tree connects all vertices of a weighted graph with the smallest total edge cost. This chapter implements Kahn's algorithm, DFS-based topological sort, Kruskal's algorithm and Prim's algorithm.
- [Chapter 14: Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union) in JavaScript: Path Compression and Union by Rank](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/union-find-disjoint-set): Union-Find, also called disjoint set union (DSU), keeps track of which elements belong to the same group and can merge two groups or check whether two elements are connected almost instantly. This chapter builds it in JavaScript, then adds union by rank and path compression, which together bring each operation down to amortized O(α(n)), effectively constant time.
- [Chapter 15: Sorting Algorithms in JavaScript: Merge Sort, Quick Sort, Heap Sort and More](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/sorting-algorithms-javascript): Sorting algorithms put elements in order, and they differ in speed, memory use and stability. This chapter implements bubble, selection and insertion sort, then merge sort, quick sort and heap sort, and finally counting and radix sort, which beat the O(n log n) limit for comparison sorts. It also explains how JavaScript's Array.prototype.sort works under the hood.
- [Chapter 16: Binary Search Patterns: Boundaries, Rotated Arrays and Binary Search on the Answer](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/binary-search-patterns): Binary search finds a target in sorted data by halving the search range at every step, which takes O(log n) time. Its real power is broader: any problem with a monotonic yes/no condition can be binary searched. This chapter covers correct boundary handling, first and last occurrence, rotated sorted arrays, binary search on the answer and searching 2D matrices.
- [Chapter 17: Backtracking in JavaScript: Permutations, Combinations, N-Queens and Sudoku](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/backtracking-algorithms): Backtracking builds a solution one choice at a time and undoes the last choice as soon as it cannot lead to a valid answer. Every backtracking algorithm follows the same choose, explore and un-choose template over a decision tree. This chapter applies that template to permutations, combinations, combination sum, N-Queens, Sudoku and word search, with pruning to cut the search.
- [Chapter 18: Dynamic Programming in JavaScript, Part 1: One-Dimensional DP](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/dynamic-programming-1d): Dynamic programming solves a problem by breaking it into overlapping sub-problems, solving each one only once and reusing the stored answers. It applies when a problem has optimal substructure and overlapping sub-problems. This chapter teaches a five-step framework for any DP problem, compares top-down memoization with bottom-up tabulation, and works through four classic one-dimensional problems.
- [Chapter 19: Dynamic Programming in JavaScript, Part 2: Two-Dimensional DP](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/dynamic-programming-2d): Two-dimensional dynamic programming uses a table indexed by two values, such as positions in two strings or an item and a remaining capacity. This chapter applies the same five-step DP framework to grid path counting, longest common subsequence, edit distance and the 0/1 knapsack problem, and shows how to reduce each table to a single row.
- [Chapter 20: Greedy Algorithms in JavaScript: When the Local Best Is the Global Best](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/greedy-algorithms): A greedy algorithm builds a solution by always taking the choice that looks best right now, never reconsidering it. It is only correct when the problem has the greedy-choice property and optimal substructure. This chapter shows where greedy fails, how to prove it correct with an exchange argument, and works through activity selection, interval scheduling, Huffman coding and greedy versus DP.
- [Chapter 21: Monotonic Stack and Monotonic Queue in JavaScript](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/monotonic-stack-and-queue): A monotonic stack keeps its elements in increasing or decreasing order by popping anything that would break the order before pushing. That turns next-greater and next-smaller element problems from O(n²) into O(n). This chapter works through daily temperatures and largest rectangle in a histogram, then uses a monotonic deque to solve sliding window maximum in linear time.
- [Chapter 22: String Algorithms in JavaScript: KMP, Rabin-Karp and Suffix Structures](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/string-algorithms-kmp-rabin-karp): String matching algorithms find occurrences of a pattern inside a text faster than checking every position from scratch. KMP uses a precomputed LPS array so the text pointer never moves backwards, giving O(n + m) time, while Rabin-Karp compares rolling hashes of each window. This chapter implements both in JavaScript and introduces suffix arrays and suffix trees.
- [Chapter 23: Segment Trees and Fenwick Trees in JavaScript: Range Queries and Updates](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/segment-tree-fenwick-tree): Segment trees and Fenwick trees answer range queries, such as the sum or minimum of a subarray, while also allowing the array to change, with both operations in O(log n). This chapter builds a segment tree using the no, total and partial overlap cases, builds a compact Fenwick tree with the lowest-set-bit trick, and extends both to range updates.
- [Chapter 24: Bit Manipulation and Bitmask Dynamic Programming in JavaScript](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/bit-manipulation-bitmask-dp): Bit manipulation works directly on the binary digits of integers, which makes some operations far faster and smaller in memory. This chapter is a complete reference to JavaScript's bitwise operators and their 32-bit behaviour, a toolkit of bit tricks such as XOR cancellation and clearing the lowest set bit, how to represent sets as bitmasks, and bitmask dynamic programming.
- [Chapter 25: Mathematics for Programmers: Number Theory, Combinatorics and Game Theory](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/math-for-programmers-number-theory): Many algorithm problems rest on a small amount of mathematics. This chapter covers the number theory programmers use most (GCD and LCM with the Euclidean algorithm, primality testing, the Sieve of Eratosthenes, modular arithmetic and fast exponentiation), the combinatorics behind permutations, combinations and Pascal's triangle, and an introduction to game theory through Nim and the Sprague-Grundy theorem.
- [Chapter 26: Advanced Graph Theory: Bipartite Matching, Maximum Flow and Min-Cut](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/advanced-graph-algorithms-network-flow): Network flow algorithms find the maximum amount that can move from a source to a sink through a graph whose edges have capacities. This chapter starts with bipartite graphs and bipartite matching, builds the Ford-Fulkerson method and the Edmonds-Karp algorithm on a residual graph, and explains the max-flow min-cut theorem and how to recover the minimum cut.
- [Chapter 27: DSA for System Design: LRU Cache, Rate Limiting, B-Trees and Consistent Hashing](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/dsa-for-system-design): The data structures used in coding interviews are the same ones inside real production systems. This chapter connects them: an LRU cache built from a hash map and a doubly linked list, sliding-window and token-bucket rate limiters, B-trees behind database indexes, consistent hashing for load balancing, and distributed concepts such as Bloom filters.
- [Chapter 28: DSA Interview Preparation: Patterns, 90-Day Roadmap and Top 100 Problems](https://shivamthakur.me/learn/dsa-master/dsa-interview-preparation-roadmap): This chapter is the revision index for the whole DSA Master series. It maps problem statements to the right technique, collects every complexity in one reference table, lists the 100 most asked interview problems organized by pattern, and gives a pattern decision tree, 90-day and 180-day study plans, a mock interview protocol and a complete glossary.
